Design Criteria/Constraint: Satisfies UK and Oxford BSB animal home cage size requirements and restrictions
Description: The SnackerTracker must satisfy the most conservative legal requirements of European Union Directive 2010/63. Animal home-cages must provide at least 330cm² floor area in total and 60cm² per animal. The most restrictive cage area and height in commonly used enclosures (i.e., individually ventilated cages and small open-top cages, respectively) is 435cm² and 12cm, respectively. The SnackerTracker therefore cannot have an aerial footprint greater than 105cm² or a vertical height exceeding 12cm.
The chassis must be designed using biocompatible materials as to not cause physical (i.e., sharp edges and restrictive spaces) or chemical (i.e., non-toxic) harm to animals.
Electrically active components must be inaccessible to animals and wired correctly to prevent short-circuits or exposed connections.
The device cannot produce excessive heat which may put animals at risk (and/or confound behaviour), interfere with thermographic recording, or damage the device itself.
Operation cannot generate excessive noise, could cause animals stress. 'Noise' includes all frequencies within animals' hearing range (i.e., 1-100kHz for mice).
Devices must be calibrated to known weights and validated to ensure accurate measurement over time (i.e., no drift).
Measurements must be registered continuously to reveal patterns of animal-device interactions and food intake.
Recordings must be validated to ensure that recording times are accurate (i.e., that a second is indeed a second) and align with the date/time at which recordings took place.
Data must be reliably stored to integrated hardware for later retrieval.
Filters must be validated across a range of experimental settings to ensure that 1) appropriate software is developed, and 2) that they can be applied in combination to optimise processing.
Costs must be minimised. A similar system (i.e., the FED3, RRID:SCR_015942) is listed at €475 with material costs totalling €205. SnackerTracker costs should not exceed this (£180).
Wireless function would make devices compatible with individually ventilated cages, and otherwise avoids the use of additional cables and connection to a power supply.
The device must function over an adequate timeframe (e.g., 24 hours).

Switches could be incorporated to mark experimentally relevant events. For example, if food needs to be changed, the researcher can flip a switch to record when this took place. This would appear in the output dataset upon analysis.
The device must be easy to use experimentally (e.g., seamless software upload, calibration, cage insertion, data extraction, and data processing).
Both operational and analysis software must have an intuitive interface for user-operation. Code should include thorough error-checking.
Analysis software must be properly documented and available via open-access platforms.
The device could enable remote monitoring for quality control and animal-surveillance.
The device could enable researchers to remotely control device operation. Researchers could wirelessly start/stop recordings or command additional peripheral integrations.
Data could be stored remotely (e.g., cloud-based, in addition to local SD registration) to improve ease of data extraction.
The device may enrich the animal home-cage environment. The overhang created by the food-holder provides a space under which animals may prefer to nest.

Easy-to-incorporate additional peripheral integrations include auditory sensors, speakers, thermographic cameras, passive infrared sensors, and LED lights. Advanced integrations might involve optogenetic probes or thermal leads. These would introduce new options for control over experimental design and data collection.
